human-heart.title: Human Heart: Chamber Anatomy, Valve Mechanics & Cardiac Cycle
human-heart.subject: Biology — Zoology
objectives: Identify the 4 chambers (Right Atrium, Right Ventricle, Left Atrium, Left Ventricle) and great vessels
Trace deoxygenated venous return through pulmonary circulation and systemic ejection into the aorta
Correlate atrioventricular (tricuspid, bicuspid) and semilunar (aortic, pulmonary) valve states across systole and diastole
Identify the anatomical landmarks of the cardiac pacemaker and conduction pathways

steps.label: Joint Diastole (Passive Ventricular Filling)
steps.note: Atria and ventricles are relaxed. Deoxygenated and oxygenated blood enter atria and passively flow through open AV valves (70% filling).

steps.label: Atrial Systole
steps.note: SA node depolarizes, atria contract, pumping the remaining 30% of blood into ventricles.

steps.label: Isovolumetric Ventricular Contraction
steps.note: Ventricles contract, pressure rises, AV valves snap shut producing the FIRST heart sound (LUB / S1). All valves temporarily closed.

steps.label: Ventricular Ejection
steps.note: Ventricular pressure exceeds aortic/pulmonary trunk pressure. Semilunar valves open; blood surges into pulmonary artery and aorta.

steps.label: Isovolumetric Ventricular Relaxation
steps.note: Ventricles relax, arterial pressure closes semilunar valves producing the SECOND heart sound (DUB / S2).

hotspots.label: Right Atrium (RA)
hotspots.explanation: Receives deoxygenated venous return from SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus. Houses the Sinoatrial (SA) Node in its anterolateral wall.

hotspots.label: Right Ventricle (RV)
hotspots.explanation: Crescent-shaped chamber with moderately thick muscular wall. Ejects deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

hotspots.label: Left Atrium (LA)
hotspots.explanation: Smooth-walled posterior cardiac chamber receiving oxygenated blood directly from four pulmonary veins (two right, two left).

hotspots.label: Left Ventricle (LV)
hotspots.explanation: Conical chamber with 3x thicker myocardium than the RV. Generates systemic systolic pressure (approx 120 mmHg) to pump blood through the aorta.

hotspots.label: Aorta (Ascending & Arch)
hotspots.explanation: Largest systemic artery in the human body. Arises from the LV, gives off coronary arteries at its base, and distributes blood to systemic circulation.

hotspots.label: Atrioventricular Valves (Tricuspid & Bicuspid/Mitral)
hotspots.explanation: Tricuspid on right (3 cusps), Bicuspid/Mitral on left (2 cusps). Anchored by fibrous chordae tendineae to papillary muscles to prevent valve eversion during systole.

accessibility.description: Detailed anatomical depiction of the human heart showing internal chambers, valve dynamics, and the directional flow of systemic and pulmonary blood.
screenReaderKeyPoints: Heart has four muscular chambers: two superior atria and two inferior ventricles
Right side handles deoxygenated blood; Left side handles oxygenated blood
First heart sound (LUB) is caused by closure of AV valves; Second heart sound (DUB) by closure of semilunar valves

practiceQuestions.prompt: During ventricular systole in a healthy human heart, which of the following valve states is observed?

choices.text: Atrioventricular valves closed, semilunar valves open
Atrioventricular valves open, semilunar valves closed
Both atrioventricular and semilunar valves remain open
Both atrioventricular and semilunar valves remain closed throughout

practiceQuestions.explanation: During the ejection phase of ventricular systole, high intraventricular pressure forces the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) open, while the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) remain firmly closed to prevent backflow into the atria.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which chamber of the human heart has the thickest muscular wall and why?

choices.text: Left Ventricle, because it must generate high pressure to pump blood throughout the systemic circulation
Right Ventricle, because it must overcome high resistance in the pulmonary capillary bed
Left Atrium, because it receives blood from four separate pulmonary veins
Right Atrium, because it receives systemic venous return from both venae cavae

practiceQuestions.explanation: The myocardium of the Left Ventricle is approximately 3 times thicker than that of the Right Ventricle because it must pump blood against systemic peripheral vascular resistance (mean arterial pressure ~93 mmHg vs pulmonary pressure ~15 mmHg).

practiceQuestions.prompt: The primary pacemaker of the human heart (Sinoatrial node) is anatomically located in the wall of which structure?

choices.text: Right Atrium, near the opening of the superior vena cava
Left Ventricle, near the interventricular septum
Interatrial septum, near the coronary sinus orifice
Left Atrium, between the pulmonary veins

practiceQuestions.explanation: The SA node (pacemaker) is situated in the upper posterolateral wall of the right atrium, immediately adjacent to the entrance of the superior vena cava.

nephron.title: Nephron Ultrastructure, Ultrafiltration & Countercurrent Multiplication
nephron.subject: Biology — Zoology
objectives: Identify the anatomical zones of the nephron (Malpighian body, PCT, Henle loop, DCT, Collecting duct)
Explain the biophysics of glomerular ultrafiltration (Net Filtration Pressure ~10 mmHg)
Trace obligatory reabsorption in the PCT (100% glucose & amino acids, 70% electrolytes and water)
Understand the countercurrent multiplier mechanism in the medullary interstitium
Explain facultative water reabsorption mediated by ADH (Vasopressin) in the collecting duct

steps.label: Glomerular Ultrafiltration
steps.note: High hydrostatic pressure in glomerulus (~60 mmHg) forces plasma fluid through podocyte slit pores into Bowman capsule, creating protein-free filtrate.

steps.label: PCT Obligatory Reabsorption
steps.note: Simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium reabsorbs 100% of glucose & amino acids, 65-70% of Na+ and water back into peritubular capillaries.

steps.label: Loop of Henle Countercurrent Multiplication
steps.note: Descending limb is permeable to water but impermeable to solutes; ascending thick limb actively pumps NaCl into the medullary interstitium.

steps.label: Collecting Duct & ADH Water Sparing
steps.note: Under ADH stimulation, aquaporin-2 channels open in the collecting duct, allowing concentrated hypertonic urine (up to 1200 mOsm/L) to form.

hotspots.label: Glomerular Capillary Tuft
hotspots.explanation: High-pressure capillary bed supplied by afferent and drained by narrower efferent arteriole.

hotspots.label: Bowman Capsule & Podocytes
hotspots.explanation: Double-walled epithelial cup containing specialized podocytes with interdigitating filtration slit diaphragms.

hotspots.label: Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)
hotspots.explanation: Major site of selective reabsorption with extensive microvilli brush border and rich mitochondria.

hotspots.label: Loop of Henle (Hairpin Loop)
hotspots.explanation: Generates an osmolarity gradient from 300 mOsm/L in cortex to 1200 mOsm/L in deep renal medulla.

hotspots.label: Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)
hotspots.explanation: Site of aldosterone-mediated Na+ reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion for acid-base homeostasis.

hotspots.label: Collecting Duct
hotspots.explanation: Permeable to water under ADH regulation, determines final specific gravity and concentration of urine.

accessibility.description: Anatomical diagram of a single nephron illustrating renal corpuscle, tubular segments, and countercurrent fluid exchange.
screenReaderKeyPoints: Glomerulus filters 180 liters of fluid daily, but 99% is reabsorbed
PCT reabsorbs all filtered glucose via sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT2)
Ascending limb of Henle is impermeable to water
ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct apical membranes

practiceQuestions.prompt: Under normal physiological conditions, which segment of the nephron reabsorbs 100% of the filtered glucose and amino acids?

choices.text: Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)
Ascending thick limb of Henle
Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)
Cortical Collecting Duct

practiceQuestions.explanation: The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) has extensive brush-border microvilli and active sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT2/SGLT1) that reabsorb virtually 100% of filtered glucose and amino acids from the tubular lumen.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The descending thin limb of the Loop of Henle is functionally characterized by which permeability property?

choices.text: Permeable to water, but nearly impermeable to electrolytes (NaCl)
Impermeable to water, but actively transports NaCl
Impermeable to both water and electrolytes
Freely permeable to proteins and glucose

practiceQuestions.explanation: The descending thin limb of Henle possesses aquaporin-1 channels making it highly permeable to water, while being relatively impermeable to NaCl and urea. Water exits into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, concentrating tubular fluid.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin) concentrates urine by stimulating the insertion of which water channels in the collecting duct?

choices.text: Aquaporin-2 channels in the apical plasma membrane
Aquaporin-1 channels in the basolateral membrane
Sodium-potassium-2chloride (NKCC2) cotransporters
Epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) exclusively

practiceQuestions.explanation: ADH binds to basolateral V2 receptors on principal cells of the collecting duct, activating intracellular cAMP and causing exocytic insertion of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels into the apical luminal membrane.

gas-exchange.title: Alveolar Gas Exchange & Respiratory Membrane Diffusion
gas-exchange.subject: Biology — Zoology
objectives: Identify the 3 layers of the respiratory diffusion barrier (alveolar epithelium, basement membrane, capillary endothelium)
Quantify the partial pressure gradients driving O2 and CO2 diffusion (Fick law of diffusion)
Understand why CO2 diffuses rapidly despite a much smaller partial pressure difference (solubility factor)
Explain the role of pulmonary surfactant secreted by Type II pneumocytes

manifest.title: Alveolar Gas Diffusion & Hemoglobin Oxygenation Explorer

steps.label: Alveolar Inhalation & Oxygen Gradient
steps.note: Fresh atmospheric air arrives in alveolus with pO2 = 104 mmHg. Pulmonary capillary blood arrives deoxygenated with pO2 = 40 mmHg.

steps.label: Oxygen Crosses Respiratory Barrier
steps.note: O2 rapidly diffuses across the ultra-thin 0.2-0.5 micrometer respiratory membrane into blood plasma and binds to hemoglobin within erythrocytes.

steps.label: Carbon Dioxide Diffusion & Exhalation
steps.note: Venous blood pCO2 = 45 mmHg diffuses down its gradient into alveolar air pCO2 = 40 mmHg to be expired during exhalation.

hotspots.label: Alveolar Air Space
hotspots.explanation: Air sac containing inspired air with pO2 = 104 mmHg and pCO2 = 40 mmHg.

hotspots.label: Type I Alveolar Epithelium
hotspots.explanation: Extremely thin squamous epithelial cells covering 95% of alveolar surface area optimized for gas diffusion.

hotspots.label: Fused Basement Membrane
hotspots.explanation: Ultra-thin extracellular matrix layer (~0.2-0.5 um) separating alveolar and capillary boundaries.

hotspots.label: Pulmonary Capillary Endothelium
hotspots.explanation: Continuous capillary wall through which erythrocytes transit in single-file (~0.75 seconds transit time).

hotspots.label: Erythrocyte & Oxyhemoglobin
hotspots.explanation: Red blood cell containing hemoglobin tetramers; converts deoxygenated Hb into bright red oxyhemoglobin (HbO2).

accessibility.description: Microscopic cross-section of the human respiratory membrane showing alveolar air space, endothelial capillary boundary, and gas diffusion.
screenReaderKeyPoints: Respiratory membrane thickness is approximately 0.2 to 0.5 micrometers
pO2 in alveoli is 104 mmHg; pO2 in deoxygenated pulmonary capillary is 40 mmHg
pCO2 in capillary blood is 45 mmHg; in alveolar air it is 40 mmHg
CO2 solubility is 20-25 times higher than O2, allowing rapid equilibrium

practiceQuestions.prompt: Despite a partial pressure gradient of only 5 mmHg (45 mmHg vs 40 mmHg), carbon dioxide diffuses almost as rapidly as oxygen across the respiratory membrane because:

choices.text: CO2 has approximately 20 to 24 times greater solubility in body fluids compared to O2
CO2 molecules are actively transported by carrier proteins in pneumocytes
The respiratory membrane is twice as thick for oxygen than for carbon dioxide
Hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2 than for O2 at pulmonary temperatures

practiceQuestions.explanation: According to Graham and Fick laws, diffusion rate is directly proportional to gas solubility and inversely proportional to the square root of molecular weight. Carbon dioxide is 20-24 times more soluble in aqueous membrane fluids than oxygen, compensating for the smaller partial pressure difference.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Type II pneumocytes (great alveolar cells) synthesize and secrete which critical substance that prevents alveolar collapse at low lung volumes?

choices.text: Pulmonary Surfactant (Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine)
Carbonic Anhydrase enzyme
Mucus glycoprotein
Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) exclusively

practiceQuestions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes synthesize pulmonary surfactant, a phospholipid-protein complex (predominantly DPPC) stored in lamellar bodies. It reduces alveolar surface tension at the air-water interface, preventing atelectasis (alveolar collapse) on expiration.
